title: Time-Resolved Thermal Susceptibility Mapping via Low-Temperature Scanning Laser Microscopy
authors: Nicolas Lejeune, Simon Van der Heyde, Alejandro V. Silhanek
abstract: We present a multiharmonic lock-in detection approach that utilizes the inverse Fast Fourier Transform to reconstruct the time evolution of thermal susceptibility with high spatial resolution. The method is implemented on a custom-built, modular scanning laser microscope designed for operation in low working-distance optical cryostats and thoroughly calibrated for spatial accuracy. A demonstrative case study using a superconducting resonator highlights the capability of this technique to generate thermal images on time scales significantly shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed, thus enabling dynamic thermal characterization with high spatial fidelity. The proposed technique of low-temperature time-resolved scanning laser microscopy offers unique opportunities to explore superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures, and other low-dimensional systems.
summary: This work introduces a novel, high-resolution technique using low-temperature scanning laser microscopy combined with multiharmonic lock-in detection to map the time evolution of thermal susceptibility. By analyzing the frequency components of the photoresponse, the authors can reconstruct dynamic thermal images, enabling the measurement of heat diffusion parameters in superconducting materials. This method offers a powerful tool for characterizing thermal dynamics in low-dimensional quantum devices.
main_problem: To achieve time-resolved thermal susceptibility mapping with high spatial resolution, especially for dynamic thermal characterization on time scales shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed.
main_result: The technique successfully reconstructs time-domain thermal responses from frequency-domain harmonic data, allowing for the measurement of heat diffusion parameters like thermal diffusivity and propagation speed in superconducting structures.
method: A multiharmonic lock-in detection approach utilizing the inverse Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is employed on a custom low-temperature scanning laser microscope setup.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on superconducting resonators (e.g., Nb bridges, YBCO meanders) cooled to low temperatures, where localized laser heating induces measurable changes in electrical resistance.
key_observables: Photoresponse, local thermal susceptibility ($\Pr$), temperature profile ($\Delta T(r)$), and the time delay of the thermal response.
important_parameters: Time resolution ($\sim$ few-$\mu$s), spatial resolution, thermal diffusivity ($D$), and heat propagation speed ($v$).
main_assumptions: The reconstruction assumes the measured signal is a global dynamic susceptibility, and the analysis relies on fitting temperature responses across distinct spatial regimes (near-field, intermediate, far-field).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SLM setup, calibration using chessboards, the dependence of laser spot size on NA, and critically, the reconstruction of time-domain thermal responses (e.g., square wave $ightarrow$ saw-tooth $ightarrow$ sine wave) as a function of distance from the excitation source.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the multiharmonic lock-in technique, validates the setup using calibration standards, applies it to measure steady-state temperature profiles, and culminates in analyzing the time-dependent thermal response across various spatial regimes to extract diffusion constants.
why_interesting: The ability to map thermal susceptibility dynamically provides a powerful, non-invasive probe into energy dissipation and heat transport mechanisms in superconducting circuits, which is crucial for understanding device performance and thermal management in quantum technologies.
